answer.exemplar: The gap is the difference between what a worker now adds to the firm's output and what the worker receives in money wages: value per worker rose faster than the hourly rate, so the share the two sides split grew steadily wider. That widening margin is what converted the falling price of manufactured goods into an argument about division of the product, and it is the ground on which unions demanded a higher rate and legislators demanded a shorter day.

questions.explanation: A strong answer names the two series, output per worker and money wages, and states that they moved at different rates with the first rising faster. It should then connect the widening margin to the falling price of goods and to the demand for a larger share, which is the ground the shorter-hours campaign fought on. It should also avoid saying that real wages fell: what the report states is that wages rose more slowly than productivity, which is a claim about the pace of increase and not about an absolute decline.

questions.explanation: The difference is the direction of travel. questions.explanation: The rule is built so that the two drafts cannot be confused and neither can quietly displace the other. The convention writes, the legislature may change the text only by a two-thirds vote, and the fallback makes the convention's text the one that returns to the voters if the legislature's is rejected — so a legislature that amends cannot also make its version the only version. answer.exemplar: Each step gives up a different kind of assurance. Labelling depends on the maker telling the truth and so cannot catch a maker who will not; inspection depends on the inspector being admitted and so cannot catch what is done when he is not there; only an analysis of a sample the government took itself does not depend on anybody else's honesty, which is why the published result is the step that can support a general rule rather than an individual case.

questions.explanation: A strong answer names the three kinds of assurance being abandoned in turn, the maker's word, then the officer's access, then nothing but the government's own test, and says that each step was taken because the previous one had proved unreliable rather than merely unhelpful. It should avoid claiming that labelling or inspection was useless: each was a stage, and the sequence shows a shift of what the state was prepared to take on trust.

questions.explanation: The clause forbids damage to the object wherever it stands and does not wait for anybody to buy the ground. A land rule would begin with the soil and require somebody to have an interest in it, so a stretch of coast or desert with no purchaser would be outside it. The permit is neither a ticket of admission nor a conveyance of title, and the second half of the statute is a separate power to set land aside, which is a different mechanism serving the same end.

answer.exemplar: Naming a substance fixes the law's target at a moment: it says what shall not be made, and a maker who substitutes something else leaves the law behind rather than disobeying it, because the word the law used is not the word on the bottle. Controlling a product instead fixes the law's target at the effect, so the question becomes what the preparation does to the user, and a substitution is caught by the question rather than by the list.

questions.explanation: A strong answer distinguishes two kinds of target. A list of named substances is complete only while nobody substitutes, and the substitution in the stem is not a violation of a naming rule but a way round it, which is what the answer has to say. The alternative is a rule addressed to the effect or the character of a preparation, where the fact that the maker changed the ingredient is irrelevant because what is regulated is still the same product sold to the same people. It should avoid saying that naming is useless, since a named substance is a clear and enforceable prohibition of the thing itself, and the failure is one of completeness rather than of force.

questions.explanation: Population growth of this speed changes the terms of a representative's job in two directions at once. The district's needs outrun the schools, the streets and the services laid out for the old number, and the men who now vote there are not the men who chose the representative in the first place, so the representative's account is owed to somebody else. That is a structural change in a constituency and not a temporary pressure on it. A new district is not a district that needs less, nothing waits for a count before a child is taught, and the mismatch between the number of children and the number of places is a matter of years rather than of one building being finished.

questions.explanation: The objection is a claim that the harm comes from the task, and the answer is that it comes from the presence. If a weaker hand is set to a job beside a stronger one, what the weaker hand can be used for affects how hard the stronger one can be driven, and an owner who needs a man's full effort cannot get it while the alternative is a child. That is why a legislature frames such a rule as a limit on hours and on the hours of the young, since the hours are the thing an owner controls and the task is not fixed in a way the law can reach. A rate difference does not separate the two men, and the owner's interest in the child's hours is the interest the law is aimed at.
